config.title: Implement UnionToIntersection type

intro.title: Implement UnionToIntersection type
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a TypeScript utility type called UnionToIntersection that transforms a union type into an intersection type. You will learn how to leverage conditional types and function type inference to achieve this transformation. The main constructs involved are generic types, conditional types (using the infer keyword), and the concept of union and intersection types in TypeScript. By the end, you will understand how to manipulate type relationships to create more precise and useful type definitions.
intro.usecase: The UnionToIntersection type is essential in advanced TypeScript libraries and component systems where you need to merge multiple configuration objects into a single, strict interface. For example, in a plugin-based dashboard, different widgets might export their own prop types as a union; converting this to an intersection ensures the host component can safely require all necessary settings. This pattern is also used in form validation libraries to combine multiple validator outputs into one consolidated error type, or in UI frameworks to merge several theme configuration objects into a single, enforceable theme contract.

objectives: Construct a generic type that accepts a union type parameter
Apply conditional types to transform union members
Implement a recursive type utility to process union types
Configure type inference to extract function parameter types
Manipulate union types to produce intersection types
Initialize the UnionToIntersection type with sample unions
Integrate the UnionToIntersection type into existing type definitions

steps.title: Import TypeScript type utilities
steps.instruction: Import the UnionToIntersection type utility from the './types' module.
steps.hint: Use the import statement with the type keyword to import a type from another file.
steps.analogousExample:
// Similar: importing a type from another module

steps.expectedOutcome: The UnionToIntersection type utility is imported and available for use in this file.
successCriteria: UnionToIntersection is imported from './types' using the type keyword.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.

steps.feedbackWrong: That's not quite right. You need to import UnionToIntersection from './types' using the type keyword.

steps.title: Create a test union type
steps.instruction: Create a union type named TestUnion with three object types: one with property 'a' of type string, one with 'b' of type number, and one with 'c' of type boolean.
steps.hint: Use the pipe operator (|) to combine multiple types into a union type.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of a union type
type Shape = Circle | Square | Triangle;
steps.seedCode:
import type { UnionToIntersection } from './types';

type TestUnion = { a: string } | { b: number } | { c: boolean };
steps.expectedOutcome: A union type TestUnion is defined with three distinct object types.
successCriteria: TestUnion is a union type containing { a: string }, { b: number }, and { c: boolean }.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close, but make sure TestUnion includes all three object types with the correct property types.
steps.feedbackWrong: That doesn't look right. Remember to create a union type with three object types using the pipe operator.

steps.title: Understand the UnionToIntersection goal
steps.instruction: Add a comment above your TestUnion type that describes what UnionToIntersection<TestUnion> should produce: an intersection of all union members.
steps.hint: Write a TypeScript comment using // or /* */ syntax. Describe that the union should become an intersection type containing all properties.
steps.analogousExample:
// This function should convert a union to an intersection
function unionToIntersection<T>() {}
steps.expectedOutcome: A clear comment explaining the transformation goal appears above the TestUnion type.
successCriteria: The comment describes that UnionToIntersection<TestUnion> should become { a: string } & { b: number } & { c: boolean }.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added a comment, but make sure it explicitly mentions that UnionToIntersection<TestUnion> should produce an intersection type containing all properties from the union.
steps.feedbackWrong: The comment doesn't describe the transformation goal. Add a comment explaining what UnionToIntersection<TestUnion> should become.

steps.title: Create the UnionToIntersection type skeleton
steps.instruction: Create the UnionToIntersection type with a generic parameter U. Start with: type UnionToIntersection<U> = ;
steps.hint: You're defining a new generic type that will take a union type U as its parameter. Leave the implementation empty for now.
steps.analogousExample:
// Similar: a generic type skeleton
type Transform<T> = ;
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have a generic type UnionToIntersection<U> defined, ready for implementation in the next steps.
successCriteria: The UnionToIntersection type is defined with a generic parameter U and an equals sign.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you've defined UnionToIntersection with a generic parameter U.

steps.title: Use conditional type distribution
steps.instruction: Inside the UnionToIntersection type definition, add a conditional type that distributes over the union: `(U extends any ? (k: U) => void : never)`
steps.hint: This conditional type will be applied to each member of the union separately. Use the syntax `U extends any ? ... : never` to create a distributive conditional type.
steps.expectedOutcome: The UnionToIntersection type now contains a distributive conditional type that will process each union member individually.
successCriteria: The UnionToIntersection type definition includes the conditional type `U extends any ? (k: U) => void : never`
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've written the exact conditional type: `U extends any ? (k: U) => void : never`
steps.feedbackWrong: add a conditional type inside UnionToIntersection that distributes over the union using `U extends any ? (k: U) => void : never`

steps.title: Extract the intersection using infer
steps.instruction: Inside the UnionToIntersection type, extend the conditional type to infer the intersection parameter I when the function type matches (k: infer I) => void.
steps.hint: Use the infer keyword to capture the type of the parameter k in the function signature.
steps.expectedOutcome: The UnionToIntersection type will now infer the intersection type I from the function parameter.
successCriteria: The UnionToIntersection type includes a conditional branch that infers I from (k: infer I) => void.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure to use the infer keyword inside the conditional type to extract the parameter type.
steps.feedbackWrong: The infer keyword is missing or incorrectly placed. Review how to infer types from function parameters.

steps.title: Complete the UnionToIntersection type
steps.instruction: Complete the UnionToIntersection type by adding the final conditional type that extracts the intersection from the distributed function signatures.
steps.hint: After the distributed conditional type (U extends any ? (k: U) => void : never), add another conditional type that checks if it extends (k: infer I) => void and returns I, otherwise never.
steps.analogousExample:
// Similar: extracting a type from a function parameter
type ExtractParam<T> = T extends (param: infer P) => any ? P : never;
steps.expectedOutcome: The UnionToIntersection type should be fully implemented, ready to transform union types into intersection types.
successCriteria: The UnionToIntersection type includes both conditional types: the distribution and the infer extraction.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you've added the second conditional type that uses infer to extract the intersection type from the function signatures.
steps.feedbackWrong: The UnionToIntersection type isn't complete yet. Remember you need to add another conditional type after the distribution to extract the intersection using infer.

steps.title: Test with function unions
steps.instruction: Create a new type alias named FuncUnion that is a union of two function types: ((x: { a: string }) => void) and ((x: { b: number }) => void).
steps.hint: Define a type alias using the 'type' keyword, then use the union operator '|' between the two function type signatures.
steps.analogousExample:

type Operation = ((value: number) => number) | ((value: string) => string);
steps.expectedOutcome: A new type alias FuncUnion is defined as a union of two function types with different parameter shapes.
successCriteria: FuncUnion type is defined as ((x: { a: string }) => void) | ((x: { b: number }) => void)
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure FuncUnion includes both function types separated by the union operator '|'.

steps.expectedOutcome: The UnionToIntersection type is exported and ready for use in other modules.
successCriteria: UnionToIntersection type is exported using export type syntax.
